source.title: Effect of data leakage in brain MRI classification using 2D convolutional neural networks
source.authors: Ekin Yağış; S. Atnafu; Alba García Seco de Herrera; Chiara Marzi; Riccardo Scheda; M. Giannelli; C. Tessa; L. Citi; S. Diciotti

page_placements.theme: Randomized-label controls reveal evaluation dependence and leakage

record.tranche_reason: The study tests random-label learning with three CNNs, but focuses on how MRI slice-level data leakage changes classification accuracy rather than reproducing the original random-label training setup.
record.gate_note: Table 4 reports training and test accuracy for OASIS-random under both subject-level and slice-level splits. Results on other datasets concern true-label classification and do not bear on these claim versions. Cited results from prior studies are excluded.
record.test_reason: Table 4 measures random-label fitting by transfer-learned CNNs in a new MRI setting. Labels are randomized per subject and shared by eight correlated slices; training uses Adam for 50 epochs with nested hyperparameter selection.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: slice-level CV severely inflates apparent classification performance, including with randomized subject labels, whereas subject-level CV yields approximately 50% test accuracy on OASIS-random. The authors recommend subject-level splitting.
record.recipe_differences: Uses transfer-learned 2D CNNs on T1-weighted brain MRI slices and compares subject-level with leakage-prone slice-level splits; it does not reproduce the original image-classification setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The split unit changes the outcome substantially: subject-level versus slice-level splitting on OASIS-random.

fits_no_version.finding: Held-out slice accuracy reaches 93.74–95.93% when training includes other slices from the same randomly labeled subjects.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Splitting correlated MRI slices from the same subjects across training and test sets can greatly inflate apparent generalization, even with subject-randomized labels.

record.problems: Only one randomized-label dataset is used. The article reports mean accuracy across outer cross-validation folds without uncertainty estimates for these results. The subject-level training accuracies vary and are not near zero error for all models.
record.rows_left_out: True-label results from OASIS-200, OASIS-34, ADNI, PPMI, and Versilia are not rows because they do not measure randomized-label learning. The study's cited prior-work results are excluded.

untested.parts: Independent random labels for individual slices; eventual fitting beyond 50 epochs; fitting without changing training hyperparameters relative to true labels, since learning rate and decay are selected through nested CV.
Relative convergence time for true versus random labels and slowing across corruption fractions. Reported aggregate runtimes do not provide these comparisons.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Training and test behavior across increasing fractions of label corruption.
Effects of adding or removing weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation.
Temporal ordering of learning real patterns and memorizing noise.

record.verdict_notes: All extracted Table 4 values are correct. Randomization is per subject, not independently per input slice. Incomplete fitting at a fixed training budget does not establish inability to fit with longer training. Leakage-driven test accuracy does not challenge chance performance on independent randomly labeled examples.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, Gaussian-noise inputs, training time, label-noise fractions, regularization, or learning order.

tranche.reason: Reports random-label training and test accuracy in a new setting: transfer-learned CNNs on brain MRI slices.

source_check.notes: VGG16-v1's trainable layers are internally inconsistent: Figure 2 specifies three fully connected layers; the methods prose specifies only the final layer. Table 4 specifies fivefold nested CV, while the methods specify tenfold CV.

statements.correction: Random labels assigned per subject; eight selected slices per subject; subject-level and slice-level CV tested; learning rate and decay selected through nested CV; no independent per-slice randomization or fixed true-label-selected hyperparameter comparison reported.
statements.problem: These conditions are untested, but the paper does not explicitly list independent slice labels or unchanged selected hyperparameters as untested.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: Training accuracy remained 63.38%, 69.17%, and 84.49%, rather than near-perfect; test accuracy was near chance (R1, R2, R5, R6, R9, R10).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Training accuracy was 99.09–100%, but test accuracy was 93.74–95.93%, not chance; the authors attribute this inflated result to leakage (R3, R4, R7, R8, R11, R12).
